The print unit includes a transport path for the stock to be printed, with the transport path defining the direction in which the stock is conveyed through the print unit.

The print unit further comprises at least two suction boxes. Each suction box has one or more inlet openings, and these inlet openings are arranged so that they are at least partially oriented toward the transport path. In this way, suction can be applied in the region of the transport path in order to influence, hold, guide, or stabilize the stock during transport through the print unit.

The inlet openings of the suction boxes together extend in a transverse direction over an inlet length. This transverse direction is oriented across the transport direction of the stock. At least 80% of the inlet length corresponds to the working width of the print unit, so that the suction effect is provided over a substantial portion of the width in which printing or stock transport takes place.

The suction boxes are arranged next to one another in the transverse direction. They are configured so that each suction box can be removed individually and independently of the other suction boxes. This allows maintenance, cleaning, replacement, or inspection of one suction box without requiring removal of the remaining suction boxes.

In some embodiments, each of the suction boxes is connected to the same common suction line. The connection may be provided through respective flow connections, allowing suction to be supplied from the common suction line to the individual suction boxes. This arrangement can simplify the suction supply system while still permitting the suction boxes to be arranged and serviced independently.
outputs.L4:
A print unit for transporting stock includes a suction-assisted transport arrangement designed to guide and hold the stock securely as it moves along a transport path. The arrangement is formed by a plurality of suction boxes positioned next to one another across the width of the transport path. Each suction box has one or more inlet openings directed toward the path of the stock so that suction can be applied over a broad area. Together, the inlet openings of the suction boxes extend over a major portion of the working width of the print unit, providing reliable support and stabilization for stock of different sizes.

The suction boxes are connected to a common suction line, which supplies negative pressure to the individual boxes during operation. Although the suction boxes share the same suction source, each box is constructed so that it can be removed separately from the print unit. This modular arrangement allows an operator or technician to take out a single suction box for cleaning, inspection, repair, or replacement without having to dismantle the entire suction system. As a result, the print unit combines wide-area suction coverage with improved accessibility and simplified maintenance.

This design is particularly useful in printing or stock-handling machines where dust, ink mist, paper particles, or other contaminants may accumulate in suction components over time. By arranging several removable suction boxes side by side, the system maintains uniform suction across the stock path while reducing downtime during servicing. The common suction line also simplifies the overall construction, since multiple boxes can be supplied from one suction source rather than requiring separate suction systems for each section. The result is a transport system that is both effective in holding and guiding the stock and practical to maintain in regular production use.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called the definite article because it points to a specific person, place, thing, or idea. When we say “the book,” we are not talking about just any book—we mean a particular book that the speaker and listener understand.

Although “the” is simple, it helps make sentences clearer and more precise. For example, “I saw a dog” introduces any dog, while “I saw the dog” suggests a specific dog already known or mentioned before. This small word helps readers and listeners follow meaning, context, and importance.

“The” is used everywhere: in conversation, writing, titles, news, and literature. It may seem ordinary, but without it, English would sound incomplete and confusing. The word “the” proves that even the shortest words can have great value in language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style description of a print unit with a stock transport path and multiple removable suction boxes arranged across the working width.
counterfactuals.output:
## Patent-Style Description

### Title  
Print Unit Having a Stock Transport Path and a Plurality of Removable Suction Boxes Arranged Across a Working Width

### Technical Field  
The invention relates to a print unit for printing sheet-form or web-form stock, in particular paper, cardboard, film, foil, labels, or other printable substrates. More particularly, the invention relates to a print unit having a stock transport path along which stock is conveyed through the print unit, and having a suction arrangement for stabilizing the stock during transport and/or printing.

### Background  
In printing machines, particularly digital printing machines, inkjet printing machines, flexographic printing machines, screen printing machines, or hybrid printing systems, it is often necessary to guide the stock precisely through a print zone. Stable transport is especially important when the stock is lightweight, curled, porous, corrugated, dimensionally unstable, or transported at high speed.

Vacuum or suction systems are commonly used to hold the stock against a transport surface, such as a perforated belt, a suction table, or a transport drum. However, conventional suction systems are often formed as large, integral suction chambers extending over substantially the entire machine width. Such arrangements can be difficult to clean, service, replace, or adapt to different stock widths. In addition, when only a portion of the working width is used, suction over unused regions may cause unnecessary air consumption, noise, energy loss, or contamination.

There is therefore a need for a print unit in which suction can be provided in a flexible and service-friendly manner across the working width of the stock transport path.

### Summary  
A print unit is provided comprising a stock transport path extending in a transport direction through the print unit and defining a working width transverse to the transport direction. A plurality of suction boxes are arranged across the working width, preferably side by side in a transverse direction. Each suction box is configured to apply suction to the stock transport path and is individually removable from the print unit. The suction boxes may be arranged beneath, within, or adjacent to a stock support or transport element, such as a perforated transport belt, suction plate, conveyor table, or transport drum segment.

By providing multiple removable suction boxes distributed across the working width, the print unit can be adapted to different substrate widths, suction zones can be selectively activated or deactivated, and individual suction boxes can be removed for cleaning, maintenance, replacement, or configuration without requiring removal of an entire suction table.

### Detailed Description  

In one embodiment, the print unit comprises a frame and a stock transport system configured to convey a printable stock along a stock transport path through at least one print zone. The stock transport path extends in a transport direction. A working width is defined transversely to the transport direction and corresponds to the maximum width over which stock may be transported and printed.

The stock transport system may comprise a conveyor belt, preferably a perforated or air-permeable belt, guided over rollers and driven by a drive unit. Alternatively, the stock transport system may comprise a perforated plate, a suction table, a vacuum conveyor, a drum, a chain gripper system with suction support, or another suitable stock support structure. The stock transport path may pass below one or more print heads, printing cylinders, coating units, drying units, curing units, inspection units, or other processing stations.

A suction arrangement is disposed relative to the stock transport path in such a manner that suction is applied to the stock being transported. The suction arrangement comprises a plurality of suction boxes arranged across the working width. The suction boxes may be arranged in a row extending substantially perpendicular to the transport direction. In some embodiments, the suction boxes are also arranged in multiple rows along the transport direction, thereby defining a matrix of suction boxes or suction zones.

Each suction box may comprise a housing defining an internal suction chamber. The housing may include an upper suction face facing the stock transport path. The suction face may be open, slotted, perforated, porous, or otherwise configured to allow air flow from the stock transport path into the suction chamber. In an embodiment using a perforated transport belt, the upper suction face of each suction box is positioned beneath the transport belt so that suction is transmitted through openings in the belt to the stock.

Each suction box is removable from the print unit independently of at least one other suction box. For example, each suction box may be insertable into and removable from a receiving position in the print unit in a direction transverse to the transport direction, parallel to the transport direction, downwardly from below the stock transport path, upwardly after opening a transport table, or laterally from a service side of the machine. The suction boxes may be supported by rails, slides, brackets, guide grooves, locating pins, quick-release couplings, clamps, latches, or bayonet-type fasteners.

In one embodiment, the suction boxes are removably mounted on a carrier structure extending across the working width. The carrier structure may comprise a plurality of receiving bays, each receiving bay being configured to receive one suction box. The receiving bays may define standardized interfaces so that suction boxes of different suction characteristics can be installed at selected positions. For instance, suction boxes having different chamber volumes, different suction face geometries, different flow resistances, or different pressure control elements may be interchanged.

Each suction box may be fluidically connectable to a vacuum source. The vacuum source may comprise a vacuum pump, fan, blower, ejector, central vacuum manifold, or another negative-pressure generator. The suction boxes may be connected to the vacuum source by way of a common manifold extending across the working width, individual ducts, flexible hoses, plug-in connectors, or sealing interfaces formed between the suction box and a manifold.

In one preferred embodiment, each suction box includes a suction connection configured to engage a corresponding vacuum port when the suction box is installed. The suction connection may include a seal, such as an elastomeric gasket, O-ring, lip seal, or face seal, to provide a substantially airtight connection. Removal of the suction box may automatically disconnect the suction connection from the vacuum port.

The suction boxes may be individually controllable. For example, each suction box may be associated with a valve, flap, throttle, damper, or controllable air-flow element. The valve may be manually adjustable or controlled by a control unit of the print unit. The control unit may activate only those suction boxes located beneath a stock width currently being processed. Suction boxes outside the stock width may be deactivated or operated at a reduced suction level. This can reduce energy consumption and improve stock handling.

In another embodiment, suction boxes may be grouped into zones. Each zone may include one or more suction boxes and may be connected to a corresponding vacuum channel. The zones may be controlled based on job data, stock width, stock type, stock grammage, stock stiffness, print mode, transport speed, or sensor feedback. Sensors may detect the presence, width, position, or edge location of the stock and automatically adjust the suction applied by the suction boxes.

The removable suction boxes may facilitate cleaning of ink mist, dust, paper fibers, powder, coating residues, or other contaminants. Individual suction boxes may be withdrawn from the machine and cleaned externally. A contaminated or damaged suction box may be replaced without dismantling the entire stock transport system. This is particularly advantageous in inkjet printing systems, where overspray and aerosol deposition can accumulate in suction openings.

The suction boxes may be arranged such that adjacent suction boxes substantially abut one another across the working width. Alternatively, small gaps may be provided between adjacent suction boxes, for example to accommodate seals, partitions, structural supports, or expansion tolerances. The suction boxes may have equal widths or different widths. In one embodiment, central suction boxes are relatively wide and edge suction boxes are narrower, enabling finer adjustment near substrate edges.

The upper suction faces of the suction boxes may jointly form a suction support plane beneath the stock transport path. The suction support plane may be substantially flat or may be curved, depending on the transport geometry. If the stock transport path is defined by a belt, the suction boxes may support the belt from below, either directly or via wear strips, support ribs, or low-friction surfaces.

In some embodiments, the suction boxes include internal flow-distribution structures, such as baffles, ribs, perforated plates, screens, honeycomb structures, or flow restrictors, to promote uniform suction over the suction face. A suction box may include multiple internal compartments arranged in the transport direction, each compartment having a separate or common vacuum connection. In this manner, suction can be profiled both across the working width and along the transport direction.

The print unit may include one or more printing assemblies positioned above or adjacent the stock transport path. In an inkjet embodiment, a plurality of inkjet print heads are arranged over the stock transport path, and the removable suction boxes are positioned beneath the print heads to maintain a defined spacing between the stock and the print heads. Stable spacing is advantageous for print quality and reduces the risk of contact between the stock and the print heads.

In one embodiment, the suction boxes are removable without removing the print heads. In another embodiment, the suction boxes are removable from a lower or lateral service side while the transport belt remains installed. The transport belt may be lifted, released, or moved to a maintenance position to allow access to the suction boxes.

The suction boxes may be encoded or identifiable by the control system. For example, each suction box may include an RFID tag, barcode, mechanical coding element, electrical connector, or memory element storing information relating to suction box type, maintenance state, operating hours, or permissible installation position. The control unit may detect whether a suction box is installed and may prevent operation if a required suction box is missing or incorrectly installed.

A sealing arrangement may be provided between each suction box and the surrounding carrier structure to limit leakage. The sealing arrangement may include peripheral seals around the upper suction face, seals around vacuum ports, inter-box seals between adjacent suction boxes, or seals between the suction boxes and the underside of a suction table or conveyor belt support.

The removable nature of the suction boxes also permits the print unit to be reconfigured for different applications. For example, suction boxes having high suction flow may be installed for porous substrates, while suction boxes having lower flow or finer perforations may be installed for thin films or delicate substrates. Edge suction boxes may be replaced with boxes configured to provide increased edge hold-down for curled stock.

### Example Embodiment  
A print unit includes a machine frame supporting a perforated conveyor belt. The conveyor belt defines a stock transport path extending in a transport direction through a print zone beneath a plurality of inkjet print heads. Beneath the upper run of the conveyor belt, a suction table is formed by eight suction boxes arranged side by side across the working width of the conveyor belt.

Each suction box includes a rectangular housing having a perforated upper plate, an internal suction chamber, and a vacuum connector on a lower side. Each suction box is received in a respective bay of a transverse support frame. The suction box can be withdrawn downwardly after releasing two quick-release latches. When installed, the vacuum connector sealingly engages a corresponding port of a vacuum manifold extending along the print unit.

Each suction box is associated with an individually controllable valve. A controller receives a selected stock width from job data and opens only the valves corresponding to suction boxes located beneath the stock. The remaining suction boxes are closed or operated at reduced suction. If one suction box becomes contaminated, it can be removed and replaced without removing adjacent suction boxes or the conveyor belt.

### Advantages  
The described print unit may provide one or more of the following advantages:

1. simplified maintenance and cleaning of suction components;  
2. replacement of individual suction boxes without dismantling a full-width suction table;  
3. modular adaptation to different stock widths and stock types;  
4. reduced air consumption by deactivating unused suction zones;  
5. improved control of stock flatness and position in the print zone;  
6. reduced contamination and easier removal of deposits from suction openings;  
7. flexible configuration of suction characteristics across the working width; and  
8. improved serviceability of wide-format printing machines.

### Possible Claim-Style Formulation  

1. A print unit comprising:  
   a stock transport path extending in a transport direction through the print unit and defining a working width transverse to the transport direction;  
   a printing assembly arranged to print on stock transported along the stock transport path; and  
   a suction arrangement configured to apply suction to the stock transport path,  
   wherein the suction arrangement comprises a plurality of suction boxes arranged across the working width, and wherein each of the plurality of suction boxes is removably mounted in the print unit.

2. The print unit of claim 1, wherein the suction boxes are arranged side by side in a direction transverse to the transport direction.

3. The print unit of claim 1, wherein each suction box is independently removable from the print unit without removal of an adjacent suction box.

4. The print unit of claim 1, wherein the stock transport path comprises a perforated transport belt and the suction boxes are arranged beneath an upper run of the perforated transport belt.

5. The print unit of claim 1, wherein each suction box comprises a suction chamber and a suction face directed toward the stock transport path.

6. The print unit of claim 1, wherein each suction box is connectable to a vacuum manifold by a releasable sealed connection.

7. The print unit of claim 1, wherein at least one valve is provided for selectively controlling suction applied to at least one of the suction boxes.

8. The print unit of claim 1, further comprising a control unit configured to activate selected suction boxes based on a width of stock transported along the stock transport path.

9. The print unit of claim 1, wherein the suction boxes are received in respective receiving bays of a carrier structure extending across the working width.

10. The print unit of claim 1, wherein at least one suction box is removable from a service side of the print unit while the printing assembly remains installed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please formulate claim language for a print unit having at least two suction boxes positioned side by side in the transverse direction, independently removable, with their inlets covering about 80% of the working width.
counterfactuals.output:
Below is example claim language you can adapt:

**1. A print unit comprising:**  
a support structure defining a working width in a transverse direction; and  
at least two suction boxes arranged side by side in the transverse direction within the working width,  
wherein each suction box comprises a suction inlet facing a print medium path,  
wherein the suction boxes are separately mounted to the support structure such that each suction box is independently removable from the print unit without removing another of the suction boxes, and  
wherein the suction inlets of the at least two suction boxes together extend across at least about 80% of the working width.

**2. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein the at least two suction boxes are positioned adjacent to one another in the transverse direction.

**3. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein each suction box is connected to a respective suction source or to a respective controllable suction channel.

**4. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein each suction box is independently slidable, liftable, or otherwise detachable from the support structure.

**5. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein the suction boxes are removable from an operator-access side of the print unit.

**6. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein the suction inlets together extend across at least about 85%, at least about 90%, or substantially the entire working width.

**7. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein the at least two suction boxes comprise a first suction box and a second suction box having respective inlet widths that together cover about 80% to about 100% of the working width.

**8. The print unit of claim 1,** further comprising a printhead arrangement disposed above the print medium path, wherein the suction boxes are configured to hold a print medium against a transport surface during printing.

**9. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein each suction box comprises a perforated, slotted, or porous inlet plate.

**10. The print unit of claim 1,** wherein the suction boxes are independently replaceable with suction boxes having different suction-inlet configurations.
